facts.statement: The study used single-cell RNA sequencing to examine salivary gland tissue from 17 people with Sjögren's Disease and 19 control participants.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Salivary glands from patients with Sjögren's Disease had a larger number of fibroblasts that showed high activity of genes responding to interferons.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The analysis identified six different groups of fibroblasts within the salivary glands.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: One group of fibroblasts, identified by the marker FMO2, had the strongest interferon-related gene activity and interacted with immune cells in the diseased tissue.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Another group of fibroblasts, identified by the marker KILON, expressed genes typically associated with nerves and axons.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: In experiments with mice, treating sensory neurons with the KILON protein made them more sensitive to pain signals.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The researchers confirmed their findings using microscopy of human tissue, cell cultures, and live mouse models.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The study suggests that FMO2-positive fibroblasts may communicate with myeloid immune cells.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The KILON-positive fibroblasts are a new type of nerve-associated cell that may be able to influence pain.
facts.subject: humans
